comments.author: @UntoldEarthDocs_Us
comments.text: What impressed me most wasn’t the beaches—it was seeing Muslims, Christians, Hindus, and Chinese communities actually helping each other celebrate their traditions. Do you think this kind of coexistence could work anywhere, or is Mauritius genuinely unique?

replies.author: @AUDIT252
replies.text: @UntoldEarthDocs_Us I was born there and  left when I was a school boy to join my parents in the  UK. I go back  often to visit family.  Holiday makers do not  really see how Mauritians really live. I suppose you could say that for other  countries as well.

replies.author: @UntoldEarthDocs_Us
replies.text: @AUDIT252 That’s a really interesting perspective, especially the distinction between living peacefully alongside each other and actually mixing socially through marriage and family. I also think your point about tourism vs. everyday life is important. A country can look incredibly harmonious to visitors while locals experience a much more complicated reality. Do you live in Mauritius, or did you live there in the past?

replies.text: @UntoldEarthDocs_Us Yes they do all live together. Muslims don't  marry Hindus. You might get a Chinese who might marry Christian ( creole) but its rare. The Government are using the land which they used to grow sugar cane  to built these  luxury apartments which  only the rich can afford who are white Europeans of South Africans. If you are going there for a Holiday it's fine.
